legals-mate.name: Légal's Mate
legals-mate.summary: A famous fake queen sacrifice: Legal let his queen be taken and won with two knights and a bishop in 7 moves.

notes.5: The bishop took the queen: the trap is set.
notes.8: Nxe5!! Legal leaves his queen hanging: if Black takes it, he loses the game.
notes.9: Bxd1?? The bait was swallowed. Taking the knight was correct, continuing a slightly worse game.
notes.10: Bxf7+ The count begins: the king is pulled to the center.
notes.12: Nd5# Mate with three minor pieces while Black's queen watches from d1.

legals-mate.lesson: Don't take an offered queen without calculating: most queens offered in the opening are poison.

immortal-game.name: The Immortal Game
immortal-game.summary: Anderssen sacrifices both rooks, the queen and a bishop to reach mate with just three minor pieces. The most famous game in history.

notes.2: The King's Gambit: a pawn for attacking speed, the language of romantic chess.
notes.16: Black takes pawns and pieces while White calmly builds his attack.
notes.28: Bxf4: White is ready to lose his rook to continue the attack.
notes.34: Bd6!! A bishop sacrifice that stops the black king from escaping.
notes.37: Black took another rook, but White has a forced mate.
notes.44: Be7# Mate with a bishop and two knights after sacrificing the queen and both rooks: that's why it's called the Immortal.

immortal-game.lesson: Initiative and attack are worth more than material: an opponent who hasn't finished development is dead, however much of your army he eats.

evergreen-game.name: The Evergreen Game
evergreen-game.summary: Another queen sacrifice from Anderssen, and the mate comes from a bishop standing in the heart of Black's position like a tree that never wilts.

notes.6: The Evans Gambit: White gives a pawn to steal the initiative.
notes.30: Nf6+! A fork that opens lines on the kingside.
notes.37: Qxf3 took the queen, but the game is already over: the big sacrifice is coming.
notes.40: Qxd7+!! The queen is offered to be taken, and Black is forced to take it.
notes.42: Bf5+ The bishop comes back and cuts off every escape route.
notes.46: Bxe7# Mate with bishops: six pawns and a queen for Black are of no use.

evergreen-game.lesson: The right sacrifice starts from precise calculation of the attacking lines, not from hoping the opponent errs.

opera-game.name: The Opera Game
opera-game.summary: Morphy plays against two noblemen while listening to the opera: fast development, a queen sacrifice, and mate with a bishop and a rook.

notes.7: Black lost time taking a knight instead of developing his pieces.
notes.12: Qb3 double pressure on b7 and f7: the weakest square at the start.
notes.18: Nxb5! Morphy sacrifices a piece to open the file and keep Black from castling.
notes.22: The black king is stuck in the center with no shelter, and the rooks storm in.
notes.30: Qb8+! A queen sacrifice that prepares the mate.
notes.32: Rd8# A clean mate: two pieces are enough when development is complete.

opera-game.lesson: Whoever develops fast and attacks first usually wins before move 20.

steinitz-bardeleben.name: Steinitz - von Bardeleben, Hastings 1895
steinitz-bardeleben.summary: Steinitz sacrifices his rook and paralyzes Black completely, and von Bardeleben couldn't bear the defeat so he got up and left the hall without resigning.

notes.32: **d5!** Breaking the center at exactly the right time: Black's king is still in the middle, and Steinitz opens the lines.
notes.38: **Qg4** Pressure from every side: Black suffers but holds together on the surface.
notes.42: **Rxe7+!!** The immortal rook sacrifice: if Black takes, he walks into a losing chase, so he kept refusing and suffering.
notes.46: **Rg7+** The rook can't be taken and the king turns: every move is a check without White losing anything.
notes.48: **Rxh7+** Von Bardeleben got up and left the hall! Steinitz showed the audience the forced mate: `...Kg8` `Rg7+` `Kh8` `Qh4+` `Kxg7` `Qh7+` and then `Qh8#`.

steinitz-bardeleben.lesson: The untouchable piece: sometimes the strongest threat is the one you leave hanging. When your opponent is tied up and paralyzed, free offers win.

rubinsteins-immortal.name: Rubinstein's Immortal, Lodz 1907
rubinsteins-immortal.summary: Rubinstein turns the board into a symphony: a rook sacrifice, a rook offering itself to 3 pieces, and a finish so beautiful the game is still taught today.

notes.39: **...Ng4!** The start: the knight advances and the threats around `h2` gather.
notes.41: **...Qh4!** The queen enters, and the bishop on `e4` can't be taken because of the counterplay on `h2`.
notes.43: **...Rxc3!!** The immortal sacrifice: the rook is broken to open all the attacking lines.
notes.45: **...Rd2!!** The move of the century: the rook offers itself to 3 pieces at once, and nobody can take it.
notes.49: **...Rh3!** White resigned: there is no defense against `Bxh3` or `...Rxh2#`. The hall stood to watch a masterpiece.

rubinsteins-immortal.lesson: Coordination matters more than material: every piece on the right square is stronger than a confused rook and queen. When the pieces talk to each other, the sacrifices come by themselves.

gold-coins-game.name: The Gold Coins Game
gold-coins-game.summary: Qg3!! A move that made the spectators throw gold coins onto the board: a queen offered to be taken three ways, and none of them saves White.

notes.4: Marshall breaks the center instead of defending it: his attacking style from move one.
notes.33: Bxc3 the start of harvesting pawns: Black opens the lines on the kingside.
notes.37: Nd4! The knight settles in the heart of the board and threatens forks.
notes.43: Rxh3 breaking the white shelter around the king.
notes.45: Qg3!! The legendary move: if fxg3 comes Ne2+ and Rxh1#, if hxg3 comes Ne2#, and if Qxg3 comes Nde2+ winning the queen. White resigned at once.

gold-coins-game.lesson: A move that breaks the rules of appearance (a queen to be taken?) can be the strongest move of the game if the calculation is behind it.

lasker-thomas.name: Lasker - Thomas, London 1912
lasker-thomas.summary: Lasker sacrifices his queen and drags the black king from one side of the board to the other, ending with the strangest checkmate in history: by moving his own king.

notes.18: **Qh5** The queen comes out: Lasker is preparing for the most famous sacrifice of his career.
notes.20: **Qxh7+!!** The queen is thrown into the fire! Black has to take, and the king begins a journey of terror.
notes.21: **...Kxh7** There is no refusing: and this is the first step on a trip from `h7` all the way to `g1`.
notes.26: **h4+** The king is dragged forward by force: every move is a check, and there is no time to breathe.
notes.34: **Kd2#!** Mate by moving the king! Lasker chose the strangest ending possible, and he could have mated by castling too.

lasker-thomas.lesson: The king hunt: a sacrifice that opens the king is worth it when you're sure the chase ends in mate. Calculate to the end before you sacrifice.

adams-torre.name: Adams - Torre, New Orleans 1920
adams-torre.summary: The white queen offers herself to be taken 3 times in a row, and nobody can touch her: the most famous lesson in the idea of the overloaded piece.

notes.16: **Nd5** Quiet central pressure, but the real plan is being prepared on the back rank.
notes.34: **Qg4!!** The queen offers herself for free! If Black takes, the weakness on the back rank collapses.
notes.36: **Qc4!!** Another offer: the queen circles around Black's queen, which is tied to guarding the rook.
notes.38: **Qc7!!** A third offer in a row! Black's queen is paralyzed: overloaded with guarding pieces and unable to take or escape.
notes.44: **Qxb7** Torre resigned: the back rank collapses onto `Re8` after any defense. A short game but an immortal one.

adams-torre.lesson: The overloaded piece: when one piece carries two duties, hit both at the same time - and don't be afraid to offer your queen for free if taking it is impossible.

game-of-the-century.name: The Game of the Century
game-of-the-century.summary: Fischer is 13 years old and plays a legendary queen sacrifice against one of America's strongest players: Be6, a move that entered history.

notes.20: Na4! Young Fischer attacks the queen and turns the table.
notes.24: Nxe4!! The start of the brilliant tactic: the knight unravels everything.
notes.33: Be6!! The most famous move in American chess: Fischer sacrifices his queen because the c4 bishop is pinned to the king.
notes.37: A series of consecutive checks that win back pawns and pieces while White gasps.
notes.47: The pinned knight on d1 falls, and White is now defending for his king's skin.
notes.77: Rc2# Mate at the end: a 13-year-old boy taught the grown-ups a lesson.

game-of-the-century.lesson: Pins and forks are the weapon of the small against the big: a piece pinned to the king has no defensive value.

fischer-spassky-g6.name: Fischer - Spassky 1972, Game 6
fischer-spassky-g6.summary: Fischer plays an opening completely unlike his style and delivers a masterpiece of the center: pawns that look broken turn into a storm of attack. Spassky stood and applauded after the resignation.

notes.0: Fischer had almost never played `c4` before: Spassky and his team prepared only for `e4`, and all the preparation went to waste.
notes.37: **...fxe6** The doubled pawns on the e file look weak, but Fischer sees that the dark squares around them will be his playground.
notes.38: **e4!** Without rushing: Fischer builds a center and chokes Black's plans piece by piece.
notes.60: **e6!** The pawn breaks in: the black structure that was solid begins to crack.
notes.74: **Rxf6!** The deciding rook sacrifice: the king's pawns are broken and the knight is removed from its best square.
notes.80: **Qf4** and Spassky resigned here: the mate is coming with no defense, and the audience and Spassky himself applauded Fischer.

fischer-spassky-g6.lesson: A structural weakness isn't always a real weakness: what decides the value of pawns is the pieces behind them and the squares they control, not how they look in the structure.

octopus-knight.name: The Octopus Knight
octopus-knight.summary: Game 16 of the 1985 World Championship: Kasparov's knight on `d3` becomes the most famous knight in history - it paralyzes all of Karpov's pieces.

notes.15: **...d5!** Kasparov breaks Karpov's center with a calculated pawn sacrifice.
notes.31: **...Nd3** The octopus knight arrives: from `d3` it paralyzes both rooks, the queen and everything.
notes.35: **...b4!** Karpov can't find a useful move - the white pieces have gone back home.
notes.65: **...Ne4** The second knight joins the attack and Karpov is forced to give a rook.
notes.79: **...Re1+** and Karpov resigned: the loss is decided. This game turned the whole World Championship around.

octopus-knight.lesson: A supported knight in the heart of the opponent's camp that can't be kicked out is stronger than a rook: the pieces around it are working, and the opponent's pieces are decoration.

karpov-kasparov-g24.name: Karpov - Kasparov 1985, Game 24
karpov-kasparov-g24.summary: The last game of the 1985 World Championship: Kasparov as Black needed only a draw to take the title, but chose to attack and win in a spectacular way from the heart of the Sicilian.

notes.28: Karpov attacks with `g4-g5` on the kingside: he must win the game to keep the title, so there's no room for caution.
notes.49: **...f5!** Kasparov answers the wing attack with a break in the center: the golden rule against flank attacks.
notes.61: **...g5!** A bold break: the black king is exposed, but the counterattack became faster than White's attack.
notes.67: **...Nxc2!** The knight jumps into the heart of the white camp and all the tactics explode in Black's favor.
notes.83: **...Nd4** and Karpov resigned: Kasparov became the 13th world champion at age 22, the youngest champion in history at that time.

karpov-kasparov-g24.lesson: When your opponent attacks your kingside, the strongest reply is often a break in the center or a faster counterattack: don't move to his rhythm.

immortal-king-walk.name: Short - Timman 1991, The King Walk
immortal-king-walk.summary: Short wins with a mate built by his own king: he walks it from g1 to g5 in front of all of the opponent's pieces, and nobody can touch it.

notes.56: **Qf6+** The queen plants herself: the mate threat on `g7` ties all of Black's pieces to the defense.
notes.58: **h4!** The start of the crazy plan: the white king intends to come up himself to support the mate on `h6`.
notes.60: **Kh2!** The first step of the journey. An idea you don't see every day: the king is an attacking piece.
notes.64: **Kf4!!** The king walks in the middle of the board and all of Black's pieces look at him helplessly: any move opens a mate on `g7`.
notes.66: **Kg5** and Timman resigned: `Kh6` is coming and then `Qg7#` with no defense. The most famous king walk in chess history.

immortal-king-walk.lesson: When all of the opponent's pieces are tied to defending against one threat, the king can turn into an attacking piece and walk in front of the whole world.

kasparov-deepblue.name: Kasparov - Deep Blue, Game 6, 1997
kasparov-deepblue.summary: The deciding game of the most famous match between a human and a machine: Deep Blue sacrifices a knight in the opening and wins in only 19 moves, and Kasparov collapses.

notes.8: **Ng5!** Deep Blue provokes: the knight comes forward in the opening with its eye on `e6`.
notes.13: **...h6?** Kasparov rushes to kick the knight: the move he regretted.
notes.14: **Nxe6!!** The shocking sacrifice: the knight is thrown at the heart of Black's center, and the immediate capture is forbidden because of `Bg6+`.
notes.19: **...Kd8** A king with no home and no future: the machine broke Black's whole structure.
notes.32: **Bf5!** Total strangulation: Black has an extra piece but is paralyzed, and Kasparov resigned soon after.
notes.36: **c4** The end: Deep Blue won the deciding game and the match 3.5-2.5 - the first computer to beat a world champion in a full match.

kasparov-deepblue.lesson: Don't rush to kick an advanced knight: an early `...h6` can open lines that you'll pay for. And respect the machine's sacrifices: it calculates deeper than you.

kasparovs-immortal.name: Kasparov's Immortal
kasparovs-immortal.summary: Kasparov sacrifices his rook on d4 and calculates 20 moves ahead: the greatest calculated attack in the history of the game.

notes.46: Rxd4!! The brilliant sacrifice: Kasparov saw the mate ten moves before it.
notes.51: b4+! The black king is dragged out to the wilderness without protection.
notes.56: Ra7! A mate threat without a check: the peak of attacking play.
notes.60: The black king walks in the middle of the board like someone walking down the street without clothes.
notes.86: Black resigned here: the knight protects the king and the mate is inevitable.

kasparovs-immortal.lesson: The greatest attacks are calculated move by move, and a sacrifice is worth it when all your lines lead to the king.

anand-immortal.name: Anand's Immortal
anand-immortal.summary: Anand gives a master class in only 23 moves: sacrifices one after another in the classical way, and Aronian resigns with nothing gained.

notes.24: **Nxh7?!** The knight goes deep to `h7` - and Anand answers with a chain of sacrifices that never ends.
notes.29: **...Bc5!** The first sacrifice: the bishop is offered for free and the white king becomes exposed.
notes.33: **...Bxd4+!** The bishop takes with check, and the king is forced to `h1`.
notes.37: **...f5!** The `f8` knight doesn't need anyone to save it: the attack on the king matters more than material.
notes.45: **...Be3!** The last move: there's no defense against the coming `g1` mate, so Aronian resigned.

anand-immortal.lesson: When the opponent's pieces are scattered on a far edge, strike in the center at once: Anand sacrificed nearly two pieces and every piece he had left was attacking directly.
